course.title: Network Security
course.description: A complete, practical Network Security course that builds from network-security fundamentals through secure protocols, firewall and proxy policy, VPN and zero-trust access, wireless and LAN security, packet and flow analysis, Zeek and IDS concepts, internal service exposure, cloud and modern service architectures, hardening, logging, resilience, incident containment, testing, and a defensive capstone. The course emphasizes authorized, non-destructive practice and evidence-based security engineering.
prerequisites: Basic command-line familiarity is helpful but taught as needed.
An understanding that all practical testing must be authorized and limited to approved systems, networks, captures, and credentials.
learningOutcomes: Explain core network-security goals, threats, vulnerabilities, exposure, trust boundaries, and defense-in-depth.
Interpret IPv4/IPv6 addressing, routing, TCP, UDP, DNS, HTTP, and TLS from a security perspective.
Design and audit least-privilege firewall, proxy, VPN, and zero-trust access policies.
Apply VLAN, wireless, and management-plane security principles.
Analyze authorized packet captures, flow telemetry, and protocol-aware network logs.
Explain IDS/IPS detection, tuning, and network-monitoring workflows.
Secure privileged network access and reduce east-west service exposure.
Apply network-security principles to cloud, microsegmented, and identity-aware architectures.
Develop hardening baselines, logging practices, resilience plans, and incident-response runbooks.
Validate network-security controls with safe positive and negative testing and complete a defensive policy-validation capstone.

modules.title: Network Security Foundations
modules.description: Establish a threat-aware model of networks, assets, trust, and controls.

lessons.title: Security Properties and Network Trust
lessons.description: Connect confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and accountability to network controls.
learningObjectives: Identify trust boundaries in a simple topology.

notes.text: Network security protects communications, infrastructure, services, and identities from unauthorized access, disclosure, modification, and disruption.

items: A network segment is not automatically a trust boundary.
A control should have an explicit purpose and owner.
Defense in depth addresses different failure modes.

notes.text: Asset -> boundary -> policy -> enforcement -> monitoring

quiz.question: Which statement is most accurate?
options: A network location alone does not establish trust.
quiz.answer: A network location alone does not establish trust.
quiz.explanation: Zero-trust principles explicitly reject implicit trust based solely on network location.

summary: Connect confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and accountability to network controls.
A network segment is not automatically a trust boundary.
A control should have an explicit purpose and owner.

lessons.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, Exposure, and Risk
lessons.description: Use precise risk terminology when analyzing network weaknesses.
learningObjectives: Differentiate threat, vulnerability, exposure, and exploit.

notes.text: A vulnerability is a weakness; exposure describes reachable attack paths; a threat is a potential source of harm; exploitation uses a weakness.

items: Public exposure can increase opportunity without determining total business impact.
Compensating controls can reduce practical risk.
Risk statements should include asset, scenario, impact, and assumptions.

quiz.question: What is the key distinction between vulnerability and exposure?
options: Vulnerability is a weakness; exposure describes how reachable that weakness is.
quiz.answer: Vulnerability is a weakness; exposure describes how reachable that weakness is.
quiz.explanation: The terms describe different dimensions of the problem.

summary: Use precise risk terminology when analyzing network weaknesses.
Public exposure can increase opportunity without determining total business impact.
Compensating controls can reduce practical risk.

lessons.title: Network Assets and Attack Surface
lessons.description: Inventory network-facing assets and identify why unmanaged components create security blind spots.
learningObjectives: Identify internet-facing and internal attack surface.
Explain why inventory must include management interfaces.

notes.text: Attack surface includes reachable interfaces, services, protocols, devices, and identities. Unknown or unmanaged assets are difficult to patch, monitor, or constrain.

items: Include routers, switches, firewalls, wireless infrastructure, virtual appliances, cloud interfaces, and administrative paths.
Ownership and business criticality make inventory actionable.

notes.text: Inventory -> ownership -> exposure -> control coverage

quiz.question: Why are unmanaged network devices risky?
options: They may fall outside patching, monitoring, and access-control processes.
quiz.answer: They may fall outside patching, monitoring, and access-control processes.
quiz.explanation: Unmanaged assets create visibility and control gaps.

summary: Inventory network-facing assets and identify why unmanaged components create security blind spots.
Include routers, switches, firewalls, wireless infrastructure, virtual appliances, cloud interfaces, and administrative paths.
Ownership and business criticality make inventory actionable.

items: Independent layers should have different failure modes.
Architecture reviews should include operational processes and recovery dependencies.

notes.text:
Internet -> edge controls -> service tier -> data tier
             |
         monitoring

quiz.question: Why is defense in depth useful?
options: Different control layers can reduce the impact of an individual control failure.
It removes the need for authentication
quiz.answer: Different control layers can reduce the impact of an individual control failure.
quiz.explanation: Security is a system of controls, not one appliance.

summary: Design layered controls instead of relying on a single perimeter device.
Independent layers should have different failure modes.
Architecture reviews should include operational processes and recovery dependencies.

notes.text:
allow tcp/443 from internet to web-tier
allow tcp/22 from mgmt to admin-hosts

quiz.question: Why should port numbers not be treated as application proof?
options: Services can be configured differently, so port evidence should be correlated with application behavior.
quiz.answer: Services can be configured differently, so port evidence should be correlated with application behavior.
quiz.explanation: Ports are conventions and configuration choices.

DNSSEC can add integrity and origin authentication for signed data, but deployment requires validation support.

A = IPv4
AAAA = IPv6
CNAME = alias
MX = mail exchange

quiz.answer: AAAA

summary: Explain name resolution and how DNS data supports network defense.

lessons.title: HTTP and TLS for Secure Applications
lessons.description: Separate application-layer HTTP semantics from TLS channel protections.
learningObjectives: Explain TLS confidentiality, integrity, and certificate validation.
Identify application risks not solved by HTTPS.

notes.text: HTTP is a stateless application-level request/response protocol. TLS protects the communication channel and authenticates peers using certificate-based trust.

items: HTTPS does not grant authorization.
TLS configuration and certificate validation are essential to secure transport.

notes.text:
GET /api/status HTTP/1.1
Host: service.example.test
Accept: application/json

practicals.title: Inspect an HTTPS Connection
practicals.description: Observe the separation between HTTP semantics and TLS transport protection using an authorized site.
steps: Open an HTTPS site you are authorized to inspect.
Inspect the certificate details.
Use browser developer tools to review request and response headers.
Document which observations belong to HTTP and which belong to TLS.
practicals.solution: The student records HTTP methods/headers separately from TLS certificate and connection information.
practicals.output: A comparison table of DNS, HTTP, TLS, certificate validation, and application authorization.

quiz.question: What does TLS primarily provide?
options: A protected communication channel plus peer authentication through certificates.
quiz.answer: A protected communication channel plus peer authentication through certificates.
quiz.explanation: TLS protects transport; application controls still matter.

summary: Separate application-layer HTTP semantics from TLS channel protections.
HTTPS does not grant authorization.
TLS configuration and certificate validation are essential to secure transport.

tasks.title: Trace a Secure Application Flow
tasks.description: Document the network path of an HTTPS application from client to database.
tasks.problemStatement: For each hop, specify protocol, trust boundary, security control, logging source, and failure mode.
tasks.hint: Separate transport protection from application authorization.
tasks.solutionCode: Client -> DNS -> TLS endpoint -> reverse proxy -> app -> database; document which component enforces each security decision.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The exercise connects protocol knowledge to architecture and monitoring.

modules.title: Firewalls, Proxies, and Remote Access
modules.description: Turn security requirements into traffic policy, proxy architecture, and controlled remote administration.

lessons.title: Firewall Policy Design
lessons.description: Create least-privilege rules with explicit intent and safe defaults.

notes.text: A firewall is a device or program that controls traffic between systems with differing security postures. Policies should be explicit, documented, testable, and reviewed.

items: Rules need ownership and business purpose.
Ordering and state handling can affect outcomes.

notes.text:
1 allow internet -> web tcp/443
2 allow app -> db tcp/5432
3 deny any -> db any

quiz.question: What is a strong general default?
options: Default deny with explicitly justified exceptions.
quiz.answer: Default deny with explicitly justified exceptions.
quiz.explanation: Default-deny reduces unintended paths when paired with well-managed exceptions.

summary: Create least-privilege rules with explicit intent and safe defaults.
Rules need ownership and business purpose.
Ordering and state handling can affect outcomes.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 — Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

lessons.title: NAT and Reverse Proxies

notes.text:

tasks.title: Audit a Firewall Policy

project.name: Network Security Control Validator
project.description: A local, offline defensive tool that compares observed flow metadata with explicit allow-policy rules and produces explainable review findings.
steps: Create the project directory and save the supplied JSON and Python files.
Define an explicit allow policy for the intended network paths.
Load and validate rules and observed flows.
Match each flow against the allow policy.
Generate findings for uncovered flows without claiming maliciousness.
Run syntax checks and automated tests.
Review the output against the intended network architecture.
Document limitations and safe future improvements.

code.README.md:
# Network Security Control Validator

Local-only defensive project. It compares observed network-flow records against an explicit allow-policy dataset and reports uncovered flows for analyst review.
code.test_validator.py:
import json, subprocess, sys
from pathlib import Path
ROOT=Path(__file__).parent

def test_validator_cli():
    p=subprocess.run([sys.executable,str(ROOT/"validator.py"),str(ROOT/"rules.json"),str(ROOT/"flows.json")],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True)
    report=json.loads(p.stdout)
    assert report["flow_count"]==4
    assert report["uncovered_count"]==1

project.explanation: The capstone models a common defensive control-validation workflow: intended policy is represented explicitly, observed traffic metadata is compared to that policy, and discrepancies become review items. The matching logic uses source zone, destination zone, protocol, and destination port. This is intentionally not a network scanner or exploit tool. Its value is repeatable verification of whether observed paths align with documented policy, which connects architecture, segmentation, monitoring, and operational review.
